title: Rethinking Neural Decompilation: Candidate Selection as the Hidden Bottleneck

paper.title: Rethinking Neural Decompilation: Candidate Selection as the Hidden Bottleneck
paper.abstract: Abstract Reverse engineering obfuscated binaries is a core task in malware analysis and software security auditing. While neural decompilers based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved the readability and functional fidelity of recovered code over heuristic tools such as Ghidra and IDA Pro, a substantial gap remains between best-sample performance and practical single-output accuracy, particularly under code obfuscation. We study this gap through the lens of candidate generation and candidate selection. Using the LLM4Decompile architecture, we show that ground-truth tokens lie within the model’s top-five next-token predictions in 95.6% of positions on average and that multi-sample decoding reaches a pass@100 of 93% on HumanEval-Decompile, indicating that correct reconstructions are typically already present in the model’s sampling space. We then evaluate a generate-then-select pipeline that ranks 100 candidates per input with text-, syntax-, embedding-, consensus-, and likelihood-based selectors. Negative perplexity emerges as the strongest static selector on HumanEval-Decompile (73.3% pass@1), while execution-guided selection nearly closes the oracle gap on ExeBench (86.3% pass@1). Combined with one epoch of fine-tuning on our newly released ExeBench-Obfuscated dataset containing 362,647 obfuscated OLLVM samples, the same pipeline increases the pass@1 rate for obfuscated binaries to 88.8%, directly contradicting prior claims that released LLM4Decompile checkpoints are unsuitable for obfuscated inputs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Binary analysis is a cornerstone of modern software security, enabling critical tasks such as malware detection, vulnerability assessment, and the auditing of proprietary or legacy software [ 32 , 5 , 14 ] . A central component of these efforts is decompilation , the process of reconstructing high-level source code from machine-executable binaries [ 21 , 34 , 39 ] . While traditional decompilers like Ghidra and IDA Pro rely on expert-crafted heuristic rules to recover control flow and program logic, they frequently struggle with the inherent loss of symbolic information during compilation, often producing results that are difficult for human analysts to interpret and impossible to re-execute [ 21 , 14 ] . The recent success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the field of program analysis [ 24 , 37 , 23 ] has also motivated their application to binary decompilation. Models such as LLM4Decompile , SALT4Decompile , and ReF Decompile have demonstrated that treating decompilation as a neural machine translation task can significantly improve code readability and functional correctness [ 34 , 10 , 39 ] . However, despite these advances, a substantial gap remains between apparent code quality and executable correctness. State-of-the-art models frequently generate code that appears plausible yet fails to satisfy functional test cases. This challenge is further exacerbated by code obfuscation techniques such as Control Flow Flattening (FLA) and Bogus Control Flow (BCF), which deliberately distort program structure and obscure semantic relationships. Under these conditions, decompilation models experience severe performance degradation and may even become ineffective at recovering executable high-level code [ 34 ] . Motivated by this observation, we shift the focus from whether neural decompilers can generate correct programs to whether they can reliably identify them among multiple plausible candidates. We therefore study neural decompilation as a two-stage problem consisting of candidate generation and candidate selection. To this end, we systematically evaluate a broad range of selection strategies, including text-based, syntax-based, embedding-based, consensus-based, likelihood-based, and execution-guided approaches. Our results demonstrate that candidate selection itself constitutes a major bottleneck in practical neural decompilation: while correct programs are frequently present in the sampled candidate pool, reliably distinguishing them from superficially plausible but functionally incorrect alternatives remains challenging. At the same time, we show that simple selection mechanisms substantially improve single-output accuracy: a likelihood-based selector reaches 73.3% pass@1 on HumanEval-Decompile [ 34 ] , improving over the strongest published baseline by 6%, while execution-guided selection nearly closes the oracle gap on ExeBench at 86.3% pass@1—all without modifying the underlying decompiler architecture. Furthermore, we introduce ExeBench-Obfuscated , a large-scale dataset of 362,647 obfuscated samples generated with common OLLVM transformations. We open-source this dataset on Huggingface and our code on Github: https://github.com/UzL-ITS/rethinking-neural-decompilation . We demonstrate that multi-candidate selection, combined with targeted fine-tuning on this corpus, substantially improves the robustness of neural decompilers under obfuscation, reaching up to 88.8% pass@1 on obfuscated binaries—a setting in which released LLM4Decompile checkpoints were previously reported as unsuitable [ 34 ] . In summary, this work makes the following contributions: (1) a token-level analysis showing that correct reconstructions are largely already present in the model’s sampling space; (2) a systematic comparison of selectors that establishes negative perplexity as a new state-of-the-art static selector on HumanEval-Decompile (+6% over prior work); (3) evidence that generate-then-select, combined with one epoch of fine-tuning, makes off-the-shelf LLM4Decompile usable on obfuscated binaries; and (4) the release of ExeBench-Obfuscated , a 362,647-sample obfuscation dataset.

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: Problem Formalization. Decompilation is formally defined as the process of mapping a binary executable x x back to a high-level source representation s ′ s^{\prime} . Given an original source code s s , the compilation process can be denoted as x = 𝒞 ⁡ ( s ) x~=~\mathcal{C}(s) , where 𝒞 \mathcal{C} represents the compiler. A decompiler 𝒟 \mathcal{D} attempts to reconstruct the logic such that 𝒟 ⁡ ( x ) = s ′ \mathcal{D}(x)=s^{\prime} , where s ′ s^{\prime} is expected to maintain high semantic fidelity and functional equivalence to s s . LLM-based Decompilation. The current state-of-the-art in neural decompilation, exemplified by LLM4Decompile , treats decompilation as a sequence-to-sequence translation problem [ 34 ] . In contrast to traditional decompilers such as Ghidra or IDA Pro , which recover control-flow and types through hand-crafted heuristics [ 21 ] , a neural decompiler with parameters θ \theta learns a conditional distribution over source token sequences S = ( s 1 , … , s T ) S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{T}) given a binary-derived input x x (e.g., assembly or Ghidra pseudo-code), factorized autoregressively as P θ ​ ( S ∣ x ) = ∏ t = 1 T P θ ​ ( s t ∣ x , s < t ) , P_{\theta}(S\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P_{\theta}(s_{t}\mid x,s_{<t}), (1) and is trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of S S over a parallel corpus. At inference, each token s t s_{t} is drawn from P θ ​ ( s t ∣ x , s < t ) P_{\theta}(s_{t}\mid x,s_{<t}) until an end-of-sequence token is produced. Sampling diversity is controlled by a temperature τ ≥ 0 \tau\geq 0 that rescales this distribution: τ → 0 \tau\to 0 recovers greedy decoding, while larger τ \tau flattens it and yields more diverse outputs. Code Obfuscation. Code obfuscation refers to semantics-preserving transformations intended to make a program difficult to analyze for both humans and automated tools [ 8 ] . In this work, we focus on common techniques provided by the Obfuscator-LLVM (OLLVM) framework. Specifically, we use the following techniques: • Control Flow Flattening (FLA): replaces the original hierarchy with a dispatcher loop that hides program logic. • Bogus Control Flow (BCF): inserts opaque predicates and unreachable code blocks. • Instruction Substitution (SUB): rewrites instructions into longer, semantically equivalent sequences. • FLA+Split: combines flattening with basic-block fragmentation, further obscuring the control-flow graph.

sections.heading: 3 Experimental Methodology
sections.text: Input Ghidra/ASM LLM Candidate Pool 𝒫 = c 1 , … , c N \mathcal{P}=c_{1},\dots,c_{N} Functional Evaluation Compilation + Unit Tests Selection Text AST ⋯ \cdots Figure 1 : Overview of our pipeline. The LLM generates a pool of N N candidates from Ghidra pseudo-code or assembly, a selector ranks them and the chosen candidate is validated against unit tests. Existing neural decompilation work typically evaluates the final decoded program, thereby mixing the model’s ability to assign probability to correct code with the decoding procedure’s ability to recover it [ 34 , 10 , 39 ] . In contrast, we decompose neural decompilation into two stages: a token-level decoder, which turns an input representation into a complete candidate program by autoregressive sampling and a program-level selector, which chooses one output from a pool of independently sampled candidates. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting pipeline. Our study is guided by the following three research questions: • RQ1: Is the correct output already present in the model’s token-level distribution? • RQ2: Can multi-candidate selection improve single-output decompilation accuracy? • RQ3: Does Multi-Candidate Selection Enable Decompilation of Obfuscated Binaries?

sections.heading: 3.1 Experimental Configurations
sections.text: We follow the LLM4Decompile evaluation protocol and reuse its two benchmarks, two input representations, and matching model variants, yielding the four configurations C1–C4 listed in Table 1 , which we use throughout the remainder of the paper. Benchmarks. HumanEval-Decompile [ 34 ] contains self-contained C functions translated from HumanEval [ 6 ] and is checked against functional assertions. The ExeBench dataset [ 3 ] contains real-world C functions extracted from GitHub, including project-specific helpers and richer control flow, packaged with the I/O wrappers required to compile and execute each function. All functions in both benchmarks were evaluated at the four standard GCC optimization levels (O0, O1, O2, O3). Input representations. We consider two binary-derived inputs. Assembly listings are produced with objdump , while Ghidra pseudo-code is produced with the Ghidra Headless Analyzer, which applies Ghidra’s decompilation passes to recover a higher-level representation than raw assembly. For ExeBench, which is distributed as source code and execution wrappers rather than as a pre-decompiled corpus, we generate both representations ourselves by compiling each function at the configured optimization level and then running objdump and Ghidra Headless on the resulting binary. For the HumanEval-Decompile dataset, we use the samples from [ 34 ] . Models. Each input representation is paired with the matching LLM4De- compile variant: LLM4Decompile-End-6.7B-v1.5 for assembly inputs and LLM4- Decompile-Ref-9B-v2 for Ghidra pseudo-code inputs. sections.heading: 3.2 Token-Level Recoverability (RQ1)
sections.text: For RQ1 we measure whether the ground-truth target tokens are accessible within the model’s distribution under a forced prefix, i.e., teacher forcing. At each target position t t , the model is conditioned on the correct prefix y < t y_{<t} and produces a distribution over the vocabulary V V , in which we record the rank of the correct token, rank ⁡ ( y t ) = 1 + | { v ∈ V : P θ ​ ( v ∣ x , y < t ) > P θ ​ ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) } | . \operatorname{rank}(y_{t})=1+\left|\left\{v\in V:P_{\theta}(v\mid x,y_{<t})>P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\right\}\right|. (2) A rank of k k means the correct token is contained in the model’s top- k k predictions. To localize prediction difficulty, we additionally group ground-truth tokens into five syntactic categories: identifiers, keywords, literals, operators, and structural tokens. Identifiers include variable, function, type, and field names; keywords include control-flow constructs such as if , while , and return , as well as qualifiers such as const and static ; literals include numeric, character, and string constants; operators include arithmetic, logical, comparison, and assignment operators; and structural tokens include braces, parentheses, brackets, semicolons, and commas. For each category, we perform the same rank-based analysis and report the corresponding rank distribution. This allows us to identify the token classes that are the most difficult for the model to recover.

sections.heading: 3.3 Candidate Selection (RQ2)
sections.text: Whereas RQ1 examines whether the ground-truth token lies in the model’s distribution at each position, a reverse engineer ultimately requires a single complete program, not a sequence of token-level predictions. RQ2 therefore lifts the analysis from tokens to programs and asks whether a functionally correct candidate can be identified without access to the ground truth. Candidate generation. For each input x x we draw multiple candidates with varying temperatures τ ∈ { 0.0 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0\} , mixing high-confidence completions with progressively more diverse samples. The candidate pool 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is fixed before any selector runs, so any difference between selectors is attributable to the selection criterion rather than to sampling variance in the generator. Selection signals. We evaluate selectors from four families. Each scores against a compilable candidate c ∈ 𝒫 c\in\mathcal{P} : similarity to the input x x , agreement within the pool 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , the decompiler’s own likelihood of c c , or runtime behavior of the compiled candidate. Two baselines complete the comparison: Random selection over 𝒫 \mathcal{P} provides a no-information lower reference, while an oracle that returns any candidate passing all functional tests serves as an upper bound over the fixed pool and is therefore not deployable. All selectors are listed and described in Appendix 0.A .

sections.heading: 3.4 Obfuscation Dataset
sections.text: To evaluate whether candidate selection remains effective beyond standard, unobfuscated binaries, we require a paired dataset that exposes neural decompilers to semantics-preserving obfuscation while retaining ground-truth source code. To the best of our knowledge, no such dataset exists at the scale required for fine-tuning LLM-based decompilers. We therefore construct an obfuscation dataset based on functions from ExeBench, named ExeBench-Obfuscated . For each sample, the target function and its dependencies are combined into a compilable source file and compiled twice: once unobfuscated (used in C2/C4 of RQ2) and once through an OLLVM toolchain with one of the four obfuscation passes described in Section 2 (used in RQ3). Throughout this process, we preserve the original function code, dependency information and compilation outcomes. To improve dataset quality, we remove empty or trivial functions, i.e., functions whose bodies are empty or reduce to a bare return; statement, since such cases provide little meaningful signal for decompilation-based learning. Finally, the generated obfuscated samples are mapped back to the original ExeBench samples. This restores repository-level metadata and execution-related fields, including the original source path, I/O specification, execution wrapper, and identifier. Following Loose et al. [ 22 ] , we do not split the training and test partition randomly but by project. This prevents data snooping within a project. ExeBench-Obfuscated contains 287,790 training samples and 74,857 test samples, leading to a total of 362,647 samples.

sections.heading: 3.5 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Following prior work on neural decompilation [ 34 ] , our primary metric is functional correctness . A candidate c c is counted as correct for an input x x if it (i) compiles successfully under the evaluation harness and (ii) passes all associated functional tests within a two-second timeout; candidates that fail to compile, time out, or fail any assertion are counted as incorrect.

sections.heading: 4 Evaluation
sections.text: We present results for each research question across the four configurations described in Section 3.1 (Table 1 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 RQ1: Is the Correct Token in the Sampling Space?
sections.text: RQ1 examines whether decompilation failures arise because the model cannot represent the correct output, or because decoding fails to recover it. To this end, we analyze the model’s next-token distribution under teacher forcing and measure how often each ground-truth token appears among the model’s highest-probability predictions. Setup. We applied the teacher-forced rank analysis from Section 3.2 to each of the four configurations using 100 randomly sampled functions per configuration. At every target position, we recorded the rank of the ground-truth token under the model’s distribution. The token-category ablation followed the five-category grouping defined in Section 3.2 . The residual error concentrates where one would expect: identifiers and the qualifier subset of keywords ( const , static , etc.) carry information that compilation discards, while operators and structural tokens, which are pinned down by the recovered control flow and expression structure, are recovered almost perfectly. Two configuration-level effects qualify this picture. The Ghidra-to-assembly switch degrades identifier recovery on ExeBench but halves the literal gap on HumanEval, which we attribute to the short, context-poor HumanEval functions rather than to assembly input in general. Second, C1’s mean rank of 15.8 — well above the 5.5–10.1 elsewhere — shows that, when the Ghidra-refined model makes errors on HumanEval, it does so definitively, with probability mass leaking far down the vocabulary. sections.heading: 4.2 RQ2: Can Selection Improve Pass@1?
sections.text: Figure 2 : Oracle pass rate versus candidate pool size k k . Curves saturate around k ∈ [ 60 , 80 ] k\in[60,80] , motivating our choice of N = 100 N=100 . RQ1 shows that the model assigns a high probability to the ground-truth tokens. However, since some information is lost during compilation, it must be estimated. In the autoregressive manner in which these models work, this means that mistakes are made, if lost information is guessed wrong [ 37 ] . RQ2 lifts the analysis from individual tokens to complete programs by asking whether a selection function applied to a pool of sampled candidates can reliably identify a functionally correct one. Pre-study: candidate pool size. Before comparing selectors, we first fix a candidate pool size N N large enough that the oracle pass rate has effectively saturated. To pick N N in a principled way, we sample 100 100 candidates per input under the temperature schedule τ ∈ { 0.0 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0\} and compute the oracle pass rate for every pool size k ∈ { 1 , … , 100 } k\in\{1,\dots,100\} . Figure 2 shows the resulting curves. All four configurations rise steeply over the first ∼ \sim 20 candidates and flatten between k = 60 k\!=\!60 and k = 80 k\!=\!80 ; beyond that point, additional samples yield at most marginal gains. However, the saturation point itself varies across configurations. We therefore fix N = 100 N=100 for the remainder of this section. This choice is intentionally conservative: it ensures that, across all four configurations, the candidate pool is saturated with respect to the model’s sampling distribution. Setup. We instantiate the generate-then-select pipeline of Section 3.3 on all four configurations from Section 3.1 . For HumanEval-Decompile (C1, C2) we use all 656 inputs (164 functions × \times 4 optimization levels); for ExeBench (C3, C4) we sample 1000 inputs uniformly. For each input we draw N = 100 N=100 candidate programs and score every candidate with each selector from Section 3.3 . However, not all samples are compilable. Therefore, the selection analysis excludes inputs for which no compilable candidate could be generated, leaving 634 (C1), 640 (C2), 774 (C3), and 428 (C4) effective inputs. Results. Table 4 reports pass@1 for every selector across the four configurations. The oracle ranges from 75.7% (C4) to 92.7% (C1), and the gap between random selection and the oracle, the empirical size of the selection bottleneck, ranges from 16.3 (C4) to 33.4 (C2) percentage points. Among static selectors, negative perplexity is the strongest on three of four configurations: C1 (73.3%, +5.1 pp over random), C2 (55.0%, +8.0 pp), and C4 (65.1%, +5.7 pp). On C3, the result is different: perplexity reaches only 70.4% against a random baseline of 69.5%, a gap that lies within sampling noise, while MBR consensus took the lead at 72.5% (+3.0 pp) and the two compile-filtered majority-vote variants followed closely at 72.2%. MBR consensus is otherwise consistently behind perplexity on the HumanEval configurations, closing 14% of the oracle–random gap on C1 (71.6%) and 15% on C2 (51.9%). Similarity-based selectors are uniformly weaker than perplexity on HumanEval; on C3 the closest similarity selectors (Edit Similarity 69.4%, Trigram 69.3%, Bigram 69.0%) cluster around the random baseline without clearly beating it. The two majority-vote variants that include non-compiling candidates (rows c, d) collapse on ExeBench, falling to 37.4% on C3 and 14.9–15.0% on C4, well below random. Execution-guided selection, the only dynamic selector evaluated, shows a sharply different profile. On HumanEval it is middling (70.8% on C1, 51.8% on C2), trailing perplexity, MBR, and both compile-filtered majority votes. On ExeBench, by contrast, it is the strongest selector by a wide margin, reaching 86.3% on C3 and 75.4% on C4—in both cases within 0.5 pp of the oracle. Candidate generation costs 0.126 s per sample on average, so a 100-candidate pool adds roughly 12.6 s of inference time per input on top of the selector cost. Discussion. The selector ranking is benchmark-dependent in a way that maps onto the candidate distribution each benchmark induces. On HumanEval-Decompile perplexity is the strongest static signal, with consensus-based selectors a step behind. On ExeBench, project-specific helpers and richer control flow push the model off its training distribution, flattening likelihoods until they no longer discriminate. This likely explains why perplexity ties with random selection on C3, and why consensus-based selectors such as MBR and compile-filtered majority vote take over there. Execution-guided selection is not affected by likelihood collapse because it evaluates candidates based on actual executions of the harness, and on ExeBench it nearly closes the oracle gap. On HumanEval-Decompile it underperforms perplexity and MBR. We attribute this to the lower complexity of HumanEval-Decompile, which weakens the discriminative power of the output-guided signal. Execution-guided selection is therefore most useful where precise input–output pairs are available. However, this condition is rarely met in real reverse-engineering settings, where static selectors offer a more realistic alternative. Orthogonally, Ghidra-input configurations (C1, C3) lead their assembly counterparts, indicating that the Ghidra front-end’s symbol- and structure-level recovery still adds value when a strong selector follows. The added inference cost is modest: at 0.126 s per sample, generating a 100-candidate pool takes roughly 12.6 s per input, which is negligible compared to the manual effort a reverse engineer would otherwise spend on the same function.

sections.heading: 4.3 RQ3: Decompilation of Obfuscated Binaries
sections.text: RQ1 and RQ2 focus on standard decompilation benchmarks, but real-world reverse engineering frequently targets binaries that have been deliberately obfuscated to hinder static analysis. RQ3 therefore asks whether the generate-then-select pipeline of RQ2 enables decompilation in this setting. The question is particularly relevant because the released LLM4Decompile checkpoints were not trained on obfuscated binaries, and the original work explicitly states that they are unsuitable for such inputs [ 34 ] . We therefore evaluate the off-the-shelf checkpoint and an obfuscation-aware fine-tuned variant with the generate-then-select pipeline from RQ2. Setup. We use LLM4Decompile-Ref-9B-v2 as the base for fine-tuning because it achieved the strongest pass@1 in configuration C1 of RQ2 and operates on Ghidra pseudo-code, the stronger input representation in our evaluation. For fine-tuning we train for a single epoch on ExeBench-Obfuscated (see Section 3.4 ). Evaluation uses 1000 random obfuscated samples covering four obfuscation classes (bcf, n = 233 n=233 ; fla, n = 208 n=208 ; fla+split, n = 251 n=251 ; sub, n = 308 n=308 ) and four optimization levels (O0, n = 219 n=219 ; O1, n = 262 n=262 ; O2, n = 235 n=235 ; O3, n = 284 n=284 ). As selection strategies we use Perplexity and Execution-guided , the best static and dynamic mechanisms from RQ2. In addition to pass@1, we report Levenstein similarity and CodeBLEU [ 28 ] to capture how closely each recovered candidate matches the ground-truth source beyond strict functional equivalence. Results. Table 5 shows that fine-tuning consistently improves performance under both selection strategies. With perplexity selection, the original model reaches 58.1% pass@1, 88.0% compile rate, 38.4% Levenshtein, and 35.9% CodeBLEU, while the fine-tuned model improves to 77.1%, 94.7%, 54.4%, and 44.4%, respectively. Execution-guided selection further increases pass@1 to 79.5% for the original model and 88.8% for the fine-tuned model, with the fine-tuned checkpoint also achieving the best overall similarity scores. Selection makes the off-the-shelf checkpoint usable on inputs it was never trained on, directly contradicting the disclaimer in the original LLM4Decompile paper [ 34 ] . Execution-guided selection retains its RQ2 advantage whenever a harness is available, and fine-tuning compounds with both selectors rather than substituting for them. The class-level breakdown is consistent with the structure of the obfuscations: sub preserves control-flow shape and therefore yields Ghidra output closest to a non-obfuscated trace, leaving the least headroom for an obfuscation-aware corpus to exploit, whereas the three control-flow transforms benefit substantially more. Across optimization levels, fine-tuning helps most where the original model struggled most, compressing the O0–O3 spread from 8.8 to 5.3 points. Moreover, because the corpus is split by project ( Section 3.4 ), the reported numbers approximate cross-project generalization rather than training data memorization.

sections.heading: 4.4 Case Study: Malware Reverse Engineering
sections.text: To illustrate the pipeline on real-world adversarial code, we applied it to a single function from the Mirai IoT botnet, a real-world malware sample [ 2 ] . We focused on toggle_obf , the routine that XOR-decrypts (and re-encrypts) entries in Mirai’s encrypted string table. We chose this function because it is the most analyst-relevant single function in the binary: a correct recovery directly exposes the XOR key, which in turn unlocks every C2 domain, command string, and kill-list entry referenced elsewhere in the bot. We compiled the leaked source code with gcc -O2 , obtained Ghidra pseudo-code for toggle_obf via the Headless Analyzer, and ran three pipelines on the same input: (i) Ghidra alone (the standard analyst baseline), (ii) the off-the-shelf LLM4Decompile-Ref-9B-v2 checkpoint with the generate-then-select configuration from RQ2 ( N = 100 N=100 candidates, perplexity selection), and (iii) the fine-tuned checkpoint from RQ3 under the same configuration. The outputs are shown side-by-side in the Appendix in Figure 3 alongside the leaked ground-truth source. The four reconstructions form a clear progression in source-level fidelity. The ground truth expresses toggle_obf as a byte-wise XOR over val->val , with the 32-bit table_key split into four single-byte subkeys and an optional DEBUG toggle. Ghidra recovers this behavior but buries it under pointer arithmetic, synthetic types, and inlined struct offsets (CodeBLEU similarity: 11.3). The off-the-shelf LLM4Decompile checkpoint with perplexity selection lifts the loop back into readable C and recovers the four masked XOR steps, though field names and struct layout remain approximate (CodeBLEU similarity: 20.1). The fine-tuned variant from Section 4.3 , with the same selection, tracks the ground truth most closely (CodeBLEU similarity: 27.0): it reproduces the four single-byte key extractions through explicit shift-and-mask expressions matching the original, and exposes the target buffer through named pointer variables rather than offset-indexed casts. Residual differences are confined to variable types and the exact form of struct field access.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Traditional and Neural Decompilation. Binary decompilation is the process of reversing machine code into high-level source code [ 32 , 14 ] . Traditional decompilers, such as Ghidra and IDA Pro , rely on hand-crafted heuristic rules and control-flow analysis to reconstruct source structures. Thus, these tools often produce output that is difficult to read, lacks meaningful variable names, and is frequently non-recompilable due to the inherent loss of symbolic information during compilation [ 21 ] . With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), decompilation has been reformulated as a neural machine translation task [ 14 ] . Early neural approaches utilized sequential models, e.g., RNNs, to learn mappings between assembly and source code [ 13 ] . Recently, LLM4Decompile established a new baseline by releasing a series of open-source models (1.3B to 22B) fine-tuned on billions of tokens [ 34 ] . Several recent works have attempted to improve upon the LLM4Decompile foundation. SccDec introduced fine-grained alignment enhancement (FAE) to better preserve original functionality [ 11 ] . ReF Decompile proposed a relabeling strategy for jump addresses and a function call mechanism to retrieve missing variable information from binaries [ 10 ] . Most recently, SALT4Decompile introduced the Source-level Abstract Logic Tree (SALT) to guide LLMs through complex control flows [ 39 ] . However, all of these efforts target the generation stage. Our work is orthogonal: we leave the underlying decompiler unchanged and instead address selection from a pool of sampled candidates. The two directions compose by construction, i.e., any improved generator slots directly into our generate-then-select pipeline. Obfuscation and Robustness Challenges. Code obfuscation has long been a fundamental obstacle for binary analysis [ 30 ] . For neural decompilers, the impact is severe: the original LLM4Decompile reports a re-executability drop of more than 70% under FLA and BCF and concludes that its checkpoints are unsuitable for obfuscated inputs [ 34 ] . Tkachenko et al. evaluate seven commercial LLMs against BCF, IS, FLA, and their combination, finding combined obfuscation defeats every model tested [ 36 ] . The problem is compounded by a lack of training data: large source-aligned corpora such as ExeBench [ 3 ] , Conan [ 25 ] or Decompile-Bench [ 35 ] contain no obfuscated samples. BinKit [ 15 ] and the Quarkslab diffing dataset [ 27 ] do provide obfuscated binaries at scale, but do not align obfuscated binaries with their original source functions, required for decompiler training. Notably, concurrently with our work, a second dataset derived from ExeBench was released [ 17 ] . Whereas our dataset employs OLLVM-based obfuscation, this dataset was generated using Tigress. The two datasets are therefore complementary, and their combined use is recommended. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we leave LLM4Decompile unchanged and study obfuscation through the lens of candidate generation and selection. We show that multi-candidate sampling with simple selectors, combined with fine-tuning on ExeBench-Obfuscated , already contradicts the unsuitability disclaimer of the original LLM4Decompile paper. To support follow-up work, we additionally release ExeBench-Obfuscated as, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale obfuscated source-to-binary dataset purpose-built for training neural decompilers. Selection versus Generation. The observation that the most-probable output of a probabilistic model is not necessarily the best one dates back to Minimum Bayes-Risk (MBR) decoding [ 16 , 9 ] . In LLM reasoning, selection has been studied through majority voting over sampled chains of thought [ 38 ] or process reward models [ 19 ] . For code, several concrete selectors have been proposed: AlphaCode clusters candidates by execution behaviour [ 18 ] , MBR-EXEC chooses the program whose traces agree most with peers [ 31 ] and Coder-Reviewer reranks with a bidirectional likelihood score [ 40 ] . A complementary line of research replaces selection with iterative repair from compiler or runtime feedback [ 7 , 26 ] . In neural decompilation, by contrast, candidate selection has received little attention. SLaDe [ 4 ] ranks samples through executable test cases, a signal similar to our execution guided selector, but unavailable for most binaries in the wild. Most current LLM-based decompilers [ 34 , 39 , 10 ] only report the output of the greedy decoding process and do not consider the search space of other candidates. We instead treat candidate selection as the object of study, systematically comparing multiple selectors. To our knowledge, this is the first study of generate-then-select pipelines for neural decompilation.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied neural decompilation as a two-stage problem of candidate generation and selection. Across our experiments, correct reconstructions are often already present in the model’s candidate space; the central challenge is identifying them reliably. Simple selection strategies substantially improve single-output accuracy, and, combined with targeted fine-tuning, make LLM4Decompile effective even on obfuscated binaries. The broader implication is that progress in neural decompilation need not come solely from larger models or more elaborate generation methods. Our results suggest that the candidate distribution produced by existing models contains considerably more useful information than greedy decoding reveals. Neural decompilation should therefore be treated not only as a generation problem, but also as a search and selection problem. Developing reliable selectors, especially ones that do not depend on execution feedback, may be as important as improving the underlying decompiler. To support follow-up work, we open-source ExeBench-Obfuscated , a corpus of 362,647 paired source-to-binary samples (287,790 training, 74,857 test).

While neural decompilers based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved the readability and functional fidelity of recovered code over heuristic tools such as Ghidra and IDA Pro, a substantial gap remains between best-sample performance and practical single-output accuracy, particularly under code obfuscation. We study this gap through the lens of candidate generation and candidate selection. Using the LLM4Decompile architecture, we show that ground-truth tokens lie within the model’s top-five next-token predictions in 95.6% of positions on average and that multi-sample decoding reaches a pass@100 of 93% on HumanEval-Decompile, indicating that correct reconstructions are typically already present in the model’s sampling space. We then evaluate a generate-then-select pipeline that ranks 100 candidates per input with text-, syntax-, embedding-, consensus-, and likelihood-based selectors. Negative perplexity emerges as the strongest static selector on HumanEval-Decompile (73.3% pass@1), while execution-guided selection nearly closes the oracle gap on ExeBench (86.3% pass@1). Combined with one epoch of fine-tuning on our newly released ExeBench-Obfuscated dataset containing 362,647 obfuscated OLLVM samples, the same pipeline increases the pass@1 rate for obfuscated binaries to 88.8%, directly contradicting prior claims that released LLM4Decompile checkpoints are unsuitable for obfuscated inputs. Keywords: Neural Decompilation Large Language Models Binary Analysis Code Obfuscation 1 Introduction Binary analysis is a cornerstone of modern software security, enabling critical tasks such as malware detection, vulnerability assessment, and the auditing of proprietary or legacy software [ 32 , 5 , 14 ] . A central component of these efforts is decompilation , the process of reconstructing high-level source code from machine-executable binaries [ 21 , 34 , 39 ] . While traditional decompilers like Ghidra and IDA Pro rely on expert-crafted heuristic rules to recover control flow and program logic, they frequently struggle with the inherent loss of symbolic information during compilation, often producing results that are difficult for human analysts to interpret and impossible to re-execute [ 21 , 14 ] . The recent success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the field of program analysis [ 24 , 37 , 23 ] has also motivated their application to binary decompilation. Models such as LLM4Decompile , SALT4Decompile , and ReF Decompile have demonstrated that treating decompilation as a neural machine translation task can significantly improve code readability and functional correctness [ 34 , 10 , 39 ] . However, despite these advances, a substantial gap remains between apparent code quality and executable correctness. State-of-the-art models frequently generate code that appears plausible yet fails to satisfy functional test cases. This challenge is further exacerbated by code obfuscation techniques such as Control Flow Flattening (FLA) and Bogus Control Flow (BCF), which deliberately distort program structure and obscure semantic relationships. Under these conditions, decompilation models experience severe performance degradation and may even become ineffective at recovering executable high-level code [ 34 ] . Motivated by this observation, we shift the focus from whether neural decompilers can generate correct programs to whether they can reliably identify them among multiple plausible candidates. We therefore study neural decompilation as a two-stage problem consisting of candidate generation and candidate selection. To this end, we systematically evaluate a broad range of selection strategies, including text-based, syntax-based, embedding-based, consensus-based, likelihood-based, and execution-guided approaches. Our results demonstrate that candidate selection itself constitutes a major bottleneck in practical neural decompilation: while correct programs are frequently present in the sampled candidate pool, reliably distinguishing them from superficially plausible but functionally incorrect alternatives remains challenging. At the same time, we show that simple selection mechanisms substantially improve single-output accuracy: a likelihood-based selector reaches 73.3% pass@1 on HumanEval-Decompile [ 34 ] , improving over the strongest published baseline by 6%, while execution-guided selection nearly closes the oracle gap on ExeBench at 86.3% pass@1—all without modifying the underlying decompiler architecture. Furthermore, we introduce ExeBench-Obfuscated , a large-scale dataset of 362,647 obfuscated samples generated with common OLLVM transformations. We open-source this dataset on Huggingface and our code on Github: https://github.com/UzL-ITS/rethinking-neural-decompilation . We demonstrate that multi-candidate selection, combined with targeted fine-tuning on this corpus, substantially improves the robustness of neural decompilers under obfuscation, reaching up to 88.8% pass@1 on obfuscated binaries—a setting in which released LLM4Decompile checkpoints were previously reported as unsuitable [ 34 ] . In summary, this work makes the following contributions: (1) a token-level analysis showing that correct reconstructions are largely already present in the model’s sampling space; (2) a systematic comparison of selectors that establishes negative perplexity as a new state-of-the-art static selector on HumanEval-Decompile (+6% over prior work); (3) evidence that generate-then-select, combined with one epoch of fine-tuning, makes off-the-shelf LLM4Decompile usable on obfuscated binaries; and (4) the release of ExeBench-Obfuscated , a 362,647-sample obfuscation dataset. 2 Background Problem Formalization. Decompilation is formally defined as the process of mapping a binary executable x x back to a high-level source representation s ′ s^{\prime} . Given an original source code s s , the compilation process can be denoted as x = 𝒞 ⁡ ( s ) x~=~\mathcal{C}(s) , where 𝒞 \mathcal{C} represents the compiler. A decompiler 𝒟 \mathcal{D} attempts to reconstruct the logic such that 𝒟 ⁡ ( x ) = s ′ \mathcal{D}(x)=s^{\prime} , where s ′ s^{\prime} is expected to maintain high semantic fidelity and functional equivalence to s s . LLM-based Decompilation. The current state-of-the-art in neural decompilation, exemplified by LLM4Decompile , treats decompilation as a sequence-to-sequence translation problem [ 34 ] . In contrast to traditional decompilers such as Ghidra or IDA Pro , which recover control-flow and types through hand-crafted heuristics [ 21 ] , a neural decompiler with parameters θ \theta learns a conditional distribution over source token sequences S = ( s 1 , … , s T ) S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{T}) given a binary-derived input x x (e.g., assembly or Ghidra pseudo-code), factorized autoregressively as P θ ​ ( S ∣ x ) = ∏ t = 1 T P θ ​ ( s t ∣ x , s < t ) , P_{\theta}(S\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P_{\theta}(s_{t}\mid x,s_{<t}), (1) and is trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of S S over a parallel corpus. At inference, each token s t s_{t} is drawn from P θ ​ ( s t ∣ x , s < t ) P_{\theta}(s_{t}\mid x,s_{<t}) until an end-of-sequence token is produced. Sampling diversity is controlled by a temperature τ ≥ 0 \tau\geq 0 that rescales this distribution: τ → 0 \tau\to 0 recovers greedy decoding, while larger τ \tau flattens it and yields more diverse outputs. Code Obfuscation. Code obfuscation refers to semantics-preserving transformations intended to make a program difficult to analyze for both humans and automated tools [ 8 ] . In this work, we focus on common techniques provided by the Obfuscator-LLVM (OLLVM) framework. Specifically, we use the following techniques: • Control Flow Flattening (FLA): replaces the original hierarchy with a dispatcher loop that hides program logic. • Bogus Control Flow (BCF): inserts opaque predicates and unreachable code blocks. • Instruction Substitution (SUB): rewrites instructions into longer, semantically equivalent sequences. • FLA+Split: combines flattening with basic-block fragmentation, further obscuring the control-flow graph. 3 Experimental Methodology Input Ghidra/ASM LLM Candidate Pool 𝒫 = c 1 , … , c N \mathcal{P}=c_{1},\dots,c_{N} Functional Evaluation Compilation + Unit Tests Selection Text AST ⋯ \cdots Figure 1 : Overview of our pipeline. The LLM generates a pool of N N candidates from Ghidra pseudo-code or assembly, a selector ranks them and the chosen candidate is validated against unit tests. Existing neural decompilation work typically evaluates the final decoded program, thereby mixing the model’s ability to assign probability to correct code with the decoding procedure’s ability to recover it [ 34 , 10 , 39 ] . In contrast, we decompose neural decompilation into two stages: a token-level decoder, which turns an input representation into a complete candidate program by autoregressive sampling and a program-level selector, which chooses one output from a pool of independently sampled candidates. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting pipeline. Our study is guided by the following three research questions: • RQ1: Is the correct output already present in the model’s token-level distribution? • RQ2: Can multi-candidate selection improve single-output decompilation accuracy? • RQ3: Does Multi-Candidate Selection Enable Decompilation of Obfuscated Binaries? 3.1 Experimental Configurations We follow the LLM4Decompile evaluation protocol and reuse its two benchmarks, two input representations, and matching model variants, yielding the four configurations C1–C4 listed in Table 1 , which we use throughout the remainder of the paper. Benchmarks. HumanEval-Decompile [ 34 ] contains self-contained C functions translated from HumanEval [ 6 ] and is checked against functional assertions. The ExeBench dataset [ 3 ] contains real-world C functions extracted from GitHub, including project-specific helpers and richer control flow, packaged with the I/O wrappers required to compile and execute each function. All functions in both benchmarks were evaluated at the four standard GCC optimization levels (O0, O1, O2, O3). Input representations. We consider two binary-derived inputs. Assembly listings are produced with objdump , while Ghidra pseudo-code is produced with the Ghidra Headless Analyzer, which applies Ghidra’s decompilation passes to recover a higher-level representation than raw assembly. For ExeBench, which is distributed as source code and execution wrappers rather than as a pre-decompiled corpus, we generate both representations ourselves by compiling each function at the configured optimization level and then running objdump and Ghidra Headless on the resulting binary. For the HumanEval-Decompile dataset, we use the samples from [ 34 ] . Models. Each input representation is paired with the matching LLM4De- compile variant: LLM4Decompile-End-6.7B-v1.5 for assembly inputs and LLM4- Decompile-Ref-9B-v2 for Ghidra pseudo-code inputs. At each target position t t , the model is conditioned on the correct prefix y < t y_{<t} and produces a distribution over the vocabulary V V , in which we record the rank of the correct token, rank ⁡ ( y t ) = 1 + | { v ∈ V : P θ ​ ( v ∣ x , y < t ) > P θ ​ ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) } | . \operatorname{rank}(y_{t})=1+\left|\left\{v\in V:P_{\theta}(v\mid x,y_{<t})>P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\right\}\right|. (2) A rank of k k means the correct token is contained in the model’s top- k k predictions. To localize prediction difficulty, we additionally group ground-truth tokens into five syntactic categories: identifiers, keywords, literals, operators, and structural tokens. Identifiers include variable, function, type, and field names; keywords include control-flow constructs such as if , while , and return , as well as qualifiers such as const and static ; literals include numeric, character, and string constants; operators include arithmetic, logical, comparison, and assignment operators; and structural tokens include braces, parentheses, brackets, semicolons, and commas. For each category, we perform the same rank-based analysis and report the corresponding rank distribution. This allows us to identify the token classes that are the most difficult for the model to recover. 3.3 Candidate Selection (RQ2) Whereas RQ1 examines whether the ground-truth token lies in the model’s distribution at each position, a reverse engineer ultimately requires a single complete program, not a sequence of token-level predictions. RQ2 therefore lifts the analysis from tokens to programs and asks whether a functionally correct candidate can be identified without access to the ground truth. Candidate generation. For each input x x we draw multiple candidates with varying temperatures τ ∈ { 0.0 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0\} , mixing high-confidence completions with progressively more diverse samples. The candidate pool 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is fixed before any selector runs, so any difference between selectors is attributable to the selection criterion rather than to sampling variance in the generator. Selection signals. We evaluate selectors from four families. Each scores against a compilable candidate c ∈ 𝒫 c\in\mathcal{P} : similarity to the input x x , agreement within the pool 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , the decompiler’s own likelihood of c c , or runtime behavior of the compiled candidate. Two baselines complete the comparison: Random selection over 𝒫 \mathcal{P} provides a no-information lower reference, while an oracle that returns any candidate passing all functional tests serves as an upper bound over the fixed pool and is therefore not deployable. All selectors are listed and described in Appendix 0.A . 3.4 Obfuscation Dataset To evaluate whether candidate selection remains effective beyond standard, unobfuscated binaries, we require a paired dataset that exposes neural decompilers to semantics-preserving obfuscation while retaining ground-truth source code. To the best of our knowledge, no such dataset exists at the scale required for fine-tuning LLM-based decompilers. We therefore construct an obfuscation dataset based on functions from ExeBench, named ExeBench-Obfuscated . For each sample, the target function and its dependencies are combined into a compilable source file and compiled twice: once unobfuscated (used in C2/C4 of RQ2) and once through an OLLVM toolchain with one of the four obfuscation passes described in Section 2 (used in RQ3). Throughout this process, we preserve the original function code, dependency information and compilation outcomes. To improve dataset quality, we remove empty or trivial functions, i.e., functions whose bodies are empty or reduce to a bare return; statement, since such cases provide little meaningful signal for decompilation-based learning. Finally, the generated obfuscated samples are mapped back to the original ExeBench samples. This restores repository-level metadata and execution-related fields, including the original source path, I/O specification, execution wrapper, and identifier. Following Loose et al. [ 22 ] , we do not split the training and test partition randomly but by project. This prevents data snooping within a project. ExeBench-Obfuscated contains 287,790 training samples and 74,857 test samples, leading to a total of 362,647 samples. 3.5 Evaluation Metrics Following prior work on neural decompilation [ 34 ] , our primary metric is functional correctness . A candidate c c is counted as correct for an input x x if it (i) compiles successfully under the evaluation harness and (ii) passes all associated functional tests within a two-second timeout; candidates that fail to compile, time out, or fail any assertion are counted as incorrect. 4 Evaluation We present results for each research question across the four configurations described in Section 3.1 (Table 1 ). 4.1 RQ1: Is the Correct Token in the Sampling Space? RQ1 examines whether decompilation failures arise because the model cannot represent the correct output, or because decoding fails to recover it. To this end, we analyze the model’s next-token distribution under teacher forcing and measure how often each ground-truth token appears among the model’s highest-probability predictions. Setup. We applied the teacher-forced rank analysis from Section 3.2 to each of the four configurations using 100 randomly sampled functions per configuration. At every target position, we recorded the rank of the ground-truth token under the model’s distribution. The token-category ablation followed the five-category grouping defined in Section 3.2 . RQ1 shows that the model assigns a high probability to the ground-truth tokens. However, since some information is lost during compilation, it must be estimated. In the autoregressive manner in which these models work, this means that mistakes are made, if lost information is guessed wrong [ 37 ] . RQ2 lifts the analysis from individual tokens to complete programs by asking whether a selection function applied to a pool of sampled candidates can reliably identify a functionally correct one. Pre-study: candidate pool size. Before comparing selectors, we first fix a candidate pool size N N large enough that the oracle pass rate has effectively saturated. To pick N N in a principled way, we sample 100 100 candidates per input under the temperature schedule τ ∈ { 0.0 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0\} and compute the oracle pass rate for every pool size k ∈ { 1 , … , 100 } k\in\{1,\dots,100\} . Figure 2 shows the resulting curves. All four configurations rise steeply over the first ∼ \sim 20 candidates and flatten between k = 60 k\!=\!60 and k = 80 k\!=\!80 ; beyond that point, additional samples yield at most marginal gains. However, the saturation point itself varies across configurations. We therefore fix N = 100 N=100 for the remainder of this section. This choice is intentionally conservative: it ensures that, across all four configurations, the candidate pool is saturated with respect to the model’s sampling distribution. Setup. We instantiate the generate-then-select pipeline of Section 3.3 on all four configurations from Section 3.1 . For HumanEval-Decompile (C1, C2) we use all 656 inputs (164 functions × \times 4 optimization levels); for ExeBench (C3, C4) we sample 1000 inputs uniformly. For each input we draw N = 100 N=100 candidate programs and score every candidate with each selector from Section 3.3 . However, not all samples are compilable. Therefore, the selection analysis excludes inputs for which no compilable candidate could be generated, leaving 634 (C1), 640 (C2), 774 (C3), and 428 (C4) effective inputs. Results. Table 4 reports pass@1 for every selector across the four configurations. The oracle ranges from 75.7% (C4) to 92.7% (C1), and the gap between random selection and the oracle, the empirical size of the selection bottleneck, ranges from 16.3 (C4) to 33.4 (C2) percentage points. Among static selectors, negative perplexity is the strongest on three of four configurations: C1 (73.3%, +5.1 pp over random), C2 (55.0%, +8.0 pp), and C4 (65.1%, +5.7 pp). On C3, the result is different: perplexity reaches only 70.4% against a random baseline of 69.5%, a gap that lies within sampling noise, while MBR consensus took the lead at 72.5% (+3.0 pp) and the two compile-filtered majority-vote variants followed closely at 72.2%. MBR consensus is otherwise consistently behind perplexity on the HumanEval configurations, closing 14% of the oracle–random gap on C1 (71.6%) and 15% on C2 (51.9%). Similarity-based selectors are uniformly weaker than perplexity on HumanEval; on C3 the closest similarity selectors (Edit Similarity 69.4%, Trigram 69.3%, Bigram 69.0%) cluster around the random baseline without clearly beating it. The two majority-vote variants that include non-compiling candidates (rows c, d) collapse on ExeBench, falling to 37.4% on C3 and 14.9–15.0% on C4, well below random. Execution-guided selection, the only dynamic selector evaluated, shows a sharply different profile. On HumanEval it is middling (70.8% on C1, 51.8% on C2), trailing perplexity, MBR, and both compile-filtered majority votes. On ExeBench, by contrast, it is the strongest selector by a wide margin, reaching 86.3% on C3 and 75.4% on C4—in both cases within 0.5 pp of the oracle. Candidate generation costs 0.126 s per sample on average, so a 100-candidate pool adds roughly 12.6 s of inference time per input on top of the selector cost. Discussion. The selector ranking is benchmark-dependent in a way that maps onto the candidate distribution each benchmark induces. On HumanEval-Decompile perplexity is the strongest static signal, with consensus-based selectors a step behind. On ExeBench, project-specific helpers and richer control flow push the model off its training distribution, flattening likelihoods until they no longer discriminate. This likely explains why perplexity ties with random selection on C3, and why consensus-based selectors such as MBR and compile-filtered majority vote take over there. Execution-guided selection is not affected by likelihood collapse because it evaluates candidates based on actual executions of the harness, and on ExeBench it nearly closes the oracle gap. On HumanEval-Decompile it underperforms perplexity and MBR. We attribute this to the lower complexity of HumanEval-Decompile, which weakens the discriminative power of the output-guided signal. Execution-guided selection is therefore most useful where precise input–output pairs are available. However, this condition is rarely met in real reverse-engineering settings, where static selectors offer a more realistic alternative. Orthogonally, Ghidra-input configurations (C1, C3) lead their assembly counterparts, indicating that the Ghidra front-end’s symbol- and structure-level recovery still adds value when a strong selector follows. The added inference cost is modest: at 0.126 s per sample, generating a 100-candidate pool takes roughly 12.6 s per input, which is negligible compared to the manual effort a reverse engineer would otherwise spend on the same function. 4.3 RQ3: Decompilation of Obfuscated Binaries RQ1 and RQ2 focus on standard decompilation benchmarks, but real-world reverse engineering frequently targets binaries that have been deliberately obfuscated to hinder static analysis. RQ3 therefore asks whether the generate-then-select pipeline of RQ2 enables decompilation in this setting. The question is particularly relevant because the released LLM4Decompile checkpoints were not trained on obfuscated binaries, and the original work explicitly states that they are unsuitable for such inputs [ 34 ] . We therefore evaluate the off-the-shelf checkpoint and an obfuscation-aware fine-tuned variant with the generate-then-select pipeline from RQ2. Setup. We use LLM4Decompile-Ref-9B-v2 as the base for fine-tuning because it achieved the strongest pass@1 in configuration C1 of RQ2 and operates on Ghidra pseudo-code, the stronger input representation in our evaluation. For fine-tuning we train for a single epoch on ExeBench-Obfuscated (see Section 3.4 ). Evaluation uses 1000 random obfuscated samples covering four obfuscation classes (bcf, n = 233 n=233 ; fla, n = 208 n=208 ; fla+split, n = 251 n=251 ; sub, n = 308 n=308 ) and four optimization levels (O0, n = 219 n=219 ; O1, n = 262 n=262 ; O2, n = 235 n=235 ; O3, n = 284 n=284 ). As selection strategies we use Perplexity and Execution-guided , the best static and dynamic mechanisms from RQ2. In addition to pass@1, we report Levenstein similarity and CodeBLEU [ 28 ] to capture how closely each recovered candidate matches the ground-truth source beyond strict functional equivalence. Selection makes the off-the-shelf checkpoint usable on inputs it was never trained on, directly contradicting the disclaimer in the original LLM4Decompile paper [ 34 ] . Execution-guided selection retains its RQ2 advantage whenever a harness is available, and fine-tuning compounds with both selectors rather than substituting for them. The class-level breakdown is consistent with the structure of the obfuscations: sub preserves control-flow shape and therefore yields Ghidra output closest to a non-obfuscated trace, leaving the least headroom for an obfuscation-aware corpus to exploit, whereas the three control-flow transforms benefit substantially more. Across optimization levels, fine-tuning helps most where the original model struggled most, compressing the O0–O3 spread from 8.8 to 5.3 points. Moreover, because the corpus is split by project ( Section 3.4 ), the reported numbers approximate cross-project generalization rather than training data memorization. 4.4 Case Study: Malware Reverse Engineering To illustrate the pipeline on real-world adversarial code, we applied it to a single function from the Mirai IoT botnet, a real-world malware sample [ 2 ] . We focused on toggle_obf , the routine that XOR-decrypts (and re-encrypts) entries in Mirai’s encrypted string table. We chose this function because it is the most analyst-relevant single function in the binary: a correct recovery directly exposes the XOR key, which in turn unlocks every C2 domain, command string, and kill-list entry referenced elsewhere in the bot. We compiled the leaked source code with gcc -O2 , obtained Ghidra pseudo-code for toggle_obf via the Headless Analyzer, and ran three pipelines on the same input: (i) Ghidra alone (the standard analyst baseline), (ii) the off-the-shelf LLM4Decompile-Ref-9B-v2 checkpoint with the generate-then-select configuration from RQ2 ( N = 100 N=100 candidates, perplexity selection), and (iii) the fine-tuned checkpoint from RQ3 under the same configuration. The outputs are shown side-by-side in the Appendix in Figure 3 alongside the leaked ground-truth source. The four reconstructions form a clear progression in source-level fidelity. The ground truth expresses toggle_obf as a byte-wise XOR over val->val , with the 32-bit table_key split into four single-byte subkeys and an optional DEBUG toggle. Ghidra recovers this behavior but buries it under pointer arithmetic, synthetic types, and inlined struct offsets (CodeBLEU similarity: 11.3). The off-the-shelf LLM4Decompile checkpoint with perplexity selection lifts the loop back into readable C and recovers the four masked XOR steps, though field names and struct layout remain approximate (CodeBLEU similarity: 20.1). The fine-tuned variant from Section 4.3 , with the same selection, tracks the ground truth most closely (CodeBLEU similarity: 27.0): it reproduces the four single-byte key extractions through explicit shift-and-mask expressions matching the original, and exposes the target buffer through named pointer variables rather than offset-indexed casts. Residual differences are confined to variable types and the exact form of struct field access. 5 Related Work Traditional and Neural Decompilation. Binary decompilation is the process of reversing machine code into high-level source code [ 32 , 14 ] . Traditional decompilers, such as Ghidra and IDA Pro , rely on hand-crafted heuristic rules and control-flow analysis to reconstruct source structures. Thus, these tools often produce output that is difficult to read, lacks meaningful variable names, and is frequently non-recompilable due to the inherent loss of symbolic information during compilation [ 21 ] . With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), decompilation has been reformulated as a neural machine translation task [ 14 ] . Early neural approaches utilized sequential models, e.g., RNNs, to learn mappings between assembly and source code [ 13 ] . Recently, LLM4Decompile established a new baseline by releasing a series of open-source models (1.3B to 22B) fine-tuned on billions of tokens [ 34 ] . Several recent works have attempted to improve upon the LLM4Decompile foundation. SccDec introduced fine-grained alignment enhancement (FAE) to better preserve original functionality [ 11 ] . ReF Decompile proposed a relabeling strategy for jump addresses and a function call mechanism to retrieve missing variable information from binaries [ 10 ] . Most recently, SALT4Decompile introduced the Source-level Abstract Logic Tree (SALT) to guide LLMs through complex control flows [ 39 ] . However, all of these efforts target the generation stage. Our work is orthogonal: we leave the underlying decompiler unchanged and instead address selection from a pool of sampled candidates. The two directions compose by construction, i.e., any improved generator slots directly into our generate-then-select pipeline. Obfuscation and Robustness Challenges. Code obfuscation has long been a fundamental obstacle for binary analysis [ 30 ] . For neural decompilers, the impact is severe: the original LLM4Decompile reports a re-executability drop of more than 70% under FLA and BCF and concludes that its checkpoints are unsuitable for obfuscated inputs [ 34 ] . Tkachenko et al. evaluate seven commercial LLMs against BCF, IS, FLA, and their combination, finding combined obfuscation defeats every model tested [ 36 ] . The problem is compounded by a lack of training data: large source-aligned corpora such as ExeBench [ 3 ] , Conan [ 25 ] or Decompile-Bench [ 35 ] contain no obfuscated samples. BinKit [ 15 ] and the Quarkslab diffing dataset [ 27 ] do provide obfuscated binaries at scale, but do not align obfuscated binaries with their original source functions, required for decompiler training. Notably, concurrently with our work, a second dataset derived from ExeBench was released [ 17 ] . Whereas our dataset employs OLLVM-based obfuscation, this dataset was generated using Tigress. The two datasets are therefore complementary, and their combined use is recommended. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we leave LLM4Decompile unchanged and study obfuscation through the lens of candidate generation and selection. We show that multi-candidate sampling with simple selectors, combined with fine-tuning on ExeBench-Obfuscated , already contradicts the unsuitability disclaimer of the original LLM4Decompile paper.
